name: Mor

catalog_locator: Section 4 'Phonology', pp. 289-291; stress/tone statement p. 290, tonal minimal pairs (1)-(14) pp. 290-291
catalog_quote: The phonemes of Mor are: t k / (b d g) / v r ? / w s h / j / m n ... + stress + tone ... I am not sure that there is any mid-high contrast in vowels in unstressed position; thus verea/veria 'arm', to.ha/tuara 'cassowary' ... Stress is unpredictable, and is written in the lexicon when there is a clear stressed syllable; but it is more likely that stress is a feature of the tonal system, which has not been fully analysed. Tonal minimal pairs abound, as the following examples show, but I have not attempted to mark tone elsewhere in this paper (' high tone, ' low tone): (1) ina 'ear' / ina 'mother' / ina 'fish' (2) i(g)wa 'cheek' / i(g)wa 'kind of fruit' ... (4) toa 'nothing' / toa 'hard, fast' ... (6) ha 'tail' / ha 'bring' (7) sariana 'heavy' / sariana 'sinks' ... (9) manana 'sweet' / manana 'body fat' ... (Elsewhere in this paper the symbol ' marks stress only.)

sources.quote: Secondary: 'Moor, which is analysed by Kamholz (2014:101-106) as having four tonal patterns, largely confined to the final two syllables. More importantly, and rather unusually for a tone language, tones are realized only on phrase-final words (Kamholz 2014:102).'
sources.locator: preprint sec. on tone languages, txt lines 73-77 (p. 2-3)

sources.citation: Kamholz, David. 2017. Tone and language contact in southern Cenderawasih Bay. NUSA: Linguistic studies of languages in and around Indonesia 62: 7-39.
sources.quote: 'Moor exhibits a word-tone system, with most words containing one of four basic tonal patterns ... tones are realized only on phrase-final words ... It is nonetheless clear from consistency among speakers that tones should be assigned at the lexical level.' Also (p. 9): suprasegmental contrasts in Moor 'are neutralized in many phonological contexts and production is quite variable'; analysis 'has not proceeded to a full-scale instrumental or phonological analysis' and 'should therefore be considered a work in progress'. Hirom dialect of Mambor.
sources.locator: Sec. 3.1 Moor, pp. 13-15, Table 2 'The four basic Moor tonal patterns'; sec. 1 pp. 8-9 on analytic status
sources.note: Published, slightly updated restatement of the Moor tone system (sec. 3.1) with explicit statement that tone is lexical but realized only phrase-finally; citable journal source for the tonal coding.

sources.citation: Kamholz, David C. 2014. Austronesians in Papua: Diversification and change in South Halmahera-West New Guinea. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. xiv+263 pp. (eScholarship qt6nj8g0b3)
sources.quote: 'Moor exhibits a word-tone system, with four basic tonal patterns ... Tone 1 (H*F) ... Tone 2 (L*R) ... Tone 3 (L*RM) ... Tone 4 (H*LH) ... the primary locus of contrast among tones 1-4 is the final two syllables. In fact, the contrast is even more restricted than this: tones are realized only on phrase-final words. As a result, the functional load of tone is quite low in discourse.' Footnote 5: 'Laycock (1978) first observed that Moor was tonal. He cited a few minimal pairs but gave no analysis.' No stress system is described for Moor; sec. 5.4 treats tone 3 as a possible reflex of Proto-SHWN
sources.locator: Ch. 5 'Tonal phonology', sec. 5.3.1 Moor, pp. 101-106 (Table 5.7 p. 102); also p. 1 ('Moor was reported to be tonal (Laycock 1978)... I determined that Moor, Yaur, and Yerisiam were all tonal')
sources.note: Fieldwork-based four-tone analysis of Moor (sec. 5.3.1) supersedes Laycock's unanalysed 1978 remark on which our coding rests; should become the deciding citation.
